place.zh: 图书馆 · 古籍部 · 十一月十九日夜
place.en: The library · the rare-books room · night of 19 November

setup.zh: 全馆停电，他和马小宝锁在古籍部一夜。九点灯灭，十点多应急灯也灭了。卫生间门里，马小宝在黑里吓坏了，越喘越急：「我手麻了……」
setup.en: The whole library blacked out, he and Ma Xiaobao locked in the rare-books room overnight. The lights died at nine, the exit sign after ten. Behind the washroom door Ma Xiaobao is terrified in the dark, panting faster and faster: "My hands are numb…"

recap.zh: 停电的古籍部，十一步，不拿眼睛走；领着马小宝吐得比吸的长。
recap.en: The blacked-out rare-books room: eleven steps, not by the eyes; leading Ma Xiaobao to breathe out longer than in.

en: Nine o'clock: the lights go out.

story.zh:
十一月十九日，星期四。中午，伤停名单发进了院队群。底下一溜「收到」，邢斌回了一个「好」，大刘回了一个大拇指。沈芒看了半天，也回了一个「收到」。

下午训练，他不想坐在场边看一群人跑，人人从他跟前过都问一句「脚咋样了」，问一回，他就得笑一回。他拄着拐去了古籍部。图书馆门口的停电通知他看过一眼，只记住了：晚上九点。

他请葛奶奶把九月那一函《养性延命录》捧出来，摊在桌上，想再看看讲吐气那几页。葛奶奶今天三点要去城里的医院拿药，一边找书一边交代管阅览室的小刘馆员：四点半闭馆，锁门，别忘了。

古籍部里还有一个人。

马小宝坐在最里头那张桌子后头，一米九三的个子塞在一把旧木椅子里，像一头熊坐进了一只茶杯。面前摊着一本线装的本草，手里攥着一支铅笔——古籍部只准带铅笔——正一笔一画地抄，抄得满头大汗。

「看什么看？」他头也不抬，「罚的。」

他那门「中药学史」的期中报告是拿软件生成的，叫老师一眼看出来了。老师也不罚别的，只罚他到古籍部照着善本手抄二十种药，一种药抄三遍，一个字不许错。

「三遍！」马小宝把铅笔在手心里掂了掂，「我家三十六家药房，哪种药我没见过？」

葛奶奶在门口那张桌子后头把老花镜往下一拉，慢悠悠地说：「见过，跟认得，是两回事。你家药房里的药，你一样一样认得，它就一样一样不坑你。」说完拎起包走了。

马小宝不吭声了，低头接着抄。两个人隔着两张桌子，谁也不理谁。阅览室里只有恒温机嗡嗡地响，匀得像有人在隔壁念经。过了很久，马小宝忽然头也不抬：「脚怎么样了？」

「疼是快不疼了。好，得几个月。」

马小宝的笔停了一停：「我高二崴过一回，三个礼拜就上场了。后来同一只脚，又崴了两回。」他接着抄，「别学我。」

这是沈芒认识马小宝以来，他说过的头一句不吓人的话。

四点二十，他把伤脚架在另一把椅子上，一本书摊在胸口，在最里头的角落里睡着了。书架挡着他，从门口望进来，只看得见一排书。四点半，小刘馆员在门口喊了一声「闭馆了啊」，没人应；她探头扫了一眼，关灯，拉上防火门，又把外头那道铁栅门「咔嗒」一声锁上了。钥匙，她带回了家。

他是被冻醒的。

阅览室里黑了一半，只有安全出口那块绿牌子亮着，和天花板底下那道采光窗里一点灰蓝的天光。他摸出手机：五点十分，没信号，Wi-Fi 也没了——闭馆的时候连路由器一块儿关了。他一瘸一拐地摸到门口，推开防火门，外头那道铁栅门锁得结结实实。他扒着铁栅栏往走廊里喊了两嗓子，只有回声。

身后「哗」一声冲水。卫生间的门开了，出来一个一米九三的人，脖子上挂着耳机，看见他，也愣住了。

「……你怎么在这儿？」两个人同时问。

马小宝戴着耳机在卫生间里待了四十来分钟——他说他是在「整理思路」——一首歌接一首歌，压根没听见有人喊闭馆。

两个人在铁栅门前头站了一会儿，能想的法子都想了一遍：手机没信号；喊，没人；铁栅门，摇得动，打不开；负一层这一头，只有古籍部。马小宝倒不慌，把灯打开了，从存包柜里拎出书包，摸出一根蛋白棒，掰了一半递过来：「行吧。熬一宿，小意思。明早开馆，馆员总得来开门。」他看了看头顶的灯，随口问，「这儿夜里不关灯吧？」

沈芒想起图书馆门口那张纸，想起他瞥过一眼、没往心里去的那几个字。

「九点，」他说，「全馆停电。」

马小宝手里那半根蛋白棒，停在了半空。

九点之前那几个钟头，两个人过得竟还不坏。

马小宝把二十种药抄完了第一遍。沈芒在书架之间一瘸一拐地转，转到第七圈，被叫住了：「你别转了，转得我眼晕。」两个人便隔着一张桌子说话。

马小宝先开的口：「哎，你天天往这儿跑，到底找什么？」

沈芒心里一跳。他找的是秘籍——这话打死也不能说。「这儿凉快。」他说，「还清净。」

「十一月了，还凉快？」马小宝嗤了一声，也不追问，把抄了一半的本子推过来，「那你考考我。抄了一下午，不知道进脑子没有。」

沈芒随手一指：「甘草。」

马小宝把本子往回一抽，翻过去了：「这个不考。」

「为什么？」

「抄得最熟。」他说得很快，一只手按在那一页上，按得指甲盖都白了。沈芒没往心里去，又指了一样；马小宝背了两句，卡住了，抓了半天脑袋，骂了自己一句，低头接着抄。

马小宝瞅着他架在椅子上的那只脚：「你天天在场边金鸡独立，闭着眼，一晃一晃的，阿禾教的？」

「嗯。脚上的线断了，得重新接上。」

「我高二那会儿，没人教我这个。」马小宝说，「教练就说，不疼了就上。」他把铅笔在桌上敲了两下，「所以我那只脚，到现在下雨还知道。」

后来他说起他爷爷，九十年代在西郊批发市场摆一个药摊，冬天手冻得裂口子，拿胶布一圈一圈地缠；一杆小秤，一钱是一钱。说起他家三十六家店，他爸一家一家地跑，一年到头不着家。沈芒没什么可说的，就听着。说着说着，两个人都不说话了。

八点五十，马小宝开始一趟一趟地看表。八点五十五，他跑去存包柜，把书包里的东西全倒在柜顶上找充电宝，没找着；手机还剩百分之九的电。沈芒那一只，下午就没电关了机。

九点整，阅览室里「嗡」的一声，恒温机停了，灯灭了。

黑没有一下子全来。安全出口那块绿牌子还亮着，靠的是里头的电池，绿莹莹一小块，照得两个人的脸都是绿的。那层薄薄的绿光里，沈芒看见马小宝坐在椅子上，两只手攥着膝盖，一动不动，眼睛盯着那块绿牌子，像怕一眨眼它就跑了。

「它能亮多久？」马小宝问。声音很平常，可平常得有点用力。

「不知道。一两个钟头吧。」

十点二十，马小宝说要去趟卫生间，打着手机的手电去了，带上了门。十点半，那块绿牌子闪了两下，灭了。

地下室没有窗，睁眼闭眼一个样。门缝底下那一线手机的光也没了——马小宝的手机也没电了。静了几秒，门里传出来一声，哑得不像他：「……沈芒？」

跟着是喘，一口赶一口，越喘越急：「我手麻了……嘴也麻了……我是不是要死了……」

一米九三的马小宝，关在黑里，吓坏了。越怕越喘，越喘手和嘴越麻，越麻越怕——他喘得停不下来。
story.en:
November 19th, Thursday. At noon the injury list went into the department-team group. A string of "received" below it; Xing Bin replied "good", Big Liu replied with a thumbs-up. Shen Mang looked at it a long while and replied "received" too.

At afternoon practice he didn't want to sit at the side watching a crowd of people run, with everyone asking "how's the foot?" as they passed, and having to smile every time. He went to the rare-books room on his crutches. He had glanced at the power-cut notice by the library door; all he had kept of it was: nine tonight.

He asked Granny Ge to bring out September's boxed set of the Yangxing Yanming Lu and lay it on the table — he wanted another look at the pages on breathing out. Granny Ge had to go into town at three to collect her medicine, and while she looked for the book she instructed Little Liu, the room attendant: close at four thirty, lock up, don't forget.

There was one other person in the room.

Ma Xiaobao sat behind the farthest table, one metre ninety-three of him wedged into an old wooden chair like a bear in a teacup. In front of him lay a thread-bound materia medica; in his hand a pencil — only pencils in the rare-books room — and he was copying, stroke by stroke, sweating all over his head.

"What are you looking at?" he said without looking up. "Punishment."

His midterm report for History of Chinese Materia Medica had been generated by an app, and the lecturer had seen through it at a glance. She didn't punish him any other way: he was to copy twenty herbs by hand from the rare editions in this room, three times each, not a character wrong.

"Three times!" Ma Xiaobao weighed the pencil in his palm. "Thirty-six pharmacies my family runs. Which of these herbs haven't I seen?"

Behind the desk by the door Granny Ge pulled her reading glasses down her nose and said slowly: "Having seen a thing and knowing it are two different things. Know every herb in your family's shops one by one, and not one of them will ever cheat you." She picked up her bag and left.

Ma Xiaobao said nothing and went back to copying. The two of them sat two tables apart, ignoring each other. The only sound in the room was the climate unit humming, as even as someone chanting sutras next door. After a long time Ma Xiaobao said, without looking up: "How's the foot?"

"Nearly stopped hurting. Healing takes months."

Ma Xiaobao's pencil paused. "I sprained mine in year eleven, and I was back on court in three weeks. Then the same foot went twice more." He went on copying. "Don't do what I did."

It was the first unfrightening sentence Shen Mang had ever heard from Ma Xiaobao.

At four twenty he propped the bad foot on another chair, laid a book open on his chest, and fell asleep in the farthest corner. The shelves screened him; from the door you saw only a row of books. At four thirty Little Liu called "closing!" from the doorway and nobody answered; she put her head in, swept a glance across, switched off the lights, pulled the fire door shut, and locked the iron grille outside with a "clack". The key, she took home.

He was woken by the cold.

The room was half dark; only the green exit sign glowed, and a little grey-blue daylight came through the narrow lightwell under the ceiling. He felt for his phone: ten past five, no signal, no Wi-Fi either — the router went off with the lights at closing. He limped to the door and pushed the fire door open: the iron grille beyond was locked solid. He clung to the bars and shouted twice down the corridor. Only the echo came back.

Behind him, a toilet flushed. The washroom door opened and out came one metre ninety-three of someone with headphones round his neck, who saw him and froze too.

"...What are you doing here?" they asked at the same moment.

Ma Xiaobao had been in the washroom with his headphones on for forty-odd minutes — "sorting out my thoughts", he said — one song after another, and never heard the call to close.

They stood at the grille a while and went through every idea they had: no signal; shouting, nobody; the grille rattled but wouldn't open; this end of the basement held nothing but the rare-books room. Ma Xiaobao wasn't fazed. He switched the lights on, pulled his bag from the locker, dug out a protein bar and broke off half for him: "Fine. One night. Easy. Come morning, the attendant has to open up." He glanced at the lights overhead. "They don't turn the lights off at night here, do they?"

Shen Mang thought of the sheet of paper by the library door, and the words he had glanced at and never taken to heart.

"Nine o'clock," he said. "Power cut. Whole building."

The half protein bar in Ma Xiaobao's hand stopped in mid-air.

The hours before nine passed better than either of them expected.

Ma Xiaobao finished the first copy of all twenty herbs. Shen Mang limped round between the shelves until, on the seventh lap, he was told: "Stop going round. You're making me dizzy." So they talked across a table.

Ma Xiaobao opened: "Hey — you come down here every day. What are you looking for?"

Shen Mang's heart jumped. He was looking for secret manuals — not a thing he would admit under torture. "It's cool in here," he said. "And quiet."

"November, and it's cool?" Ma Xiaobao snorted but didn't press. He pushed his half-filled copybook across. "Test me, then. A whole afternoon of copying — no idea if any of it got in."

Shen Mang pointed at random: "Liquorice."

Ma Xiaobao snatched the book back and turned the page: "Not that one."

"Why not?"

"Know it best." He said it fast, one hand pressed flat on the page, pressed till the nail went white. Shen Mang didn't take it in, and pointed at another; Ma Xiaobao recited two lines, stuck, scratched his head for ages, swore at himself and went back to copying.

Ma Xiaobao looked at the foot propped on the chair: "You stand there at the side of the court every day like a rooster, eyes shut, wobbling about. Ahe's idea?"

"Mm. The wires in the foot are torn. They have to be hooked up again."

"Nobody taught me that in year eleven," Ma Xiaobao said. "The coach just said: when it stops hurting, you play." He tapped the pencil twice on the table. "Which is why that foot still knows when it's going to rain."

Later he talked about his grandfather, who in the nineties kept a herb stall in the wholesale market in the western suburbs, hands cracked open by the winter cold and wound round and round with sticking plaster; one little steelyard, and a qian was a qian. He talked about the family's thirty-six shops, how his father drove from one to the next and was never home all year. Shen Mang had nothing to add, so he listened. After a while neither of them said anything.

At ten to nine Ma Xiaobao started checking the time, again and again. At five to, he ran to the locker and tipped everything in his bag onto the top of it looking for a power bank; there wasn't one. His phone had nine percent left. Shen Mang's had died that afternoon.

At nine exactly the room went "hum", the climate unit stopped, and the lights went out.

The dark didn't come all at once. The green exit sign still glowed on its battery, a small green patch that turned both their faces green. In that thin green light Shen Mang saw Ma Xiaobao sitting in his chair, both hands gripping his knees, perfectly still, eyes fixed on the sign as though it might run away if he blinked.

"How long will it last?" Ma Xiaobao asked. His voice was ordinary — ordinary with a little too much effort in it.

"Don't know. An hour or two."

At twenty past ten Ma Xiaobao said he needed the washroom, went by the light of his phone torch, and shut the door. At half past, the green sign flickered twice and went out.

The basement had no windows; eyes open or shut made no difference. The sliver of phone light under the door was gone too — Ma Xiaobao's phone had died as well. A few seconds of silence, then a voice through the door, hoarse, not like him: "...Shen Mang?"

Then the breathing, one breath chasing the next, faster and faster: "My hands have gone numb... my mouth too... am I going to die..."

Ma Xiaobao, one metre ninety-three, shut in the dark, was terrified. The more frightened, the harder he breathed; the harder he breathed, the number his hands and mouth went; the number they went, the more frightened he was — and he couldn't stop.

label.en: Stand up and go to him

exits.means: stands up and walks to him in the dark

refuse.en: Eleven steps still to go in the dark.

story.zh:
沈芒站了起来。拐滑到桌子底下，摸了两把，没摸着。从这儿到卫生间，要绕过两排书架、一张桌子，中间地上还有马小宝倒出来的一地东西。

那只右脚，是五天前崴的。

这几天他每天在宿舍闭着眼单脚站，扶着桌沿，老蔡在上铺数：三秒，六秒，十一秒——今天早上，十五秒。闭着眼，脑子看不见，只能听脚上的线说话。

现在，他闭不闭眼，都一样了。

他扶着桌沿迈出第一步。右脚落地，脚踝往外歪了一歪——他觉出来了。那根线把这一歪报了上去，腿自己往回一收，稳住了。第二步。第三步，脚背踢到了马小宝的保温杯，杯子骨碌碌滚远了。第四步，手摸到书架冰凉的铁边。他顺着书架往前蹭，一步，一步，心里数着。卫生间那头，喘气声越来越急，像有人在黑地里溺水。

第九步，碰到桌角。第十步，绕过去。第十一步，摸到了卫生间的门把手。

他站稳了。右脚踩在地上，脚踝里一阵一阵地酸，可是没歪，没倒。这十一步，他不是拿眼睛走的——眼睛在这里一点用也没有，也没有一双眼睛看着他；他走的，是脚上那些线。他在黑地里咧开嘴，没出声地喊了一句：

成了！

推开门，马小宝缩在马桶和墙中间，抱着膝盖，浑身发抖。沈芒摸着墙蹲下去，没碰他：「小宝哥。跟着我喘。吐得比吸的长。」他先吸四拍，再吐六拍，吐得黑地里听得见。马小宝跟不上，吐到一半又急急地吸；他不催，一口一口地领，像领一个刚学走路的孩子。十口，二十口。三十几口以后，马小宝哑着嗓子说：「……手不麻了。我还当是气不够，越吸越使劲。」

「是吸多了。二氧化碳吹没了，手才麻。」沈芒说，「吐慢点，攒回来。」

两个人就那么坐着，一个在门里，一个在门外，背靠着门框。后来马小宝在黑里说，小时候捉迷藏，钻进爷爷仓库一只装甘草的大木柜，柜门从外头扣上了，赶上过年，仓库锁了，人都回家了，他在里头待了一宿。「第二天早上我爷爷开柜子，我一身甘草味儿。我爸说，没事。」

沈芒想起那一页「甘草」，和按白了的指甲盖。

过了很久，马小宝说：「今天的事——」

「今天什么事？」沈芒说，「黑成这样，我什么也没看见。」

黑地里，马小宝「哧」地笑了一声，鼻子囔囔的。

六点灯亮。恒温机「嗡」地又响了起来。沈芒靠着门框被灯晃醒，看见马小宝蜷在地上睡着了，一米九三的人，睡得像一只虾。

桌上那一函《养性延命录》还摊着，昨天下午睡着了，没人收。讲吐气那一页的页边有几行铅笔字，又小又急，最上头一行：「试之。吐长于纳，心果缓。」吐得比吸的长，心就慢下来——阿禾十月里教他的，几十年前有人在这张桌子上试过了。他把函套里那张借阅卡抽出来，并排一放：跟九月里那个洇了水的名字，一个样。往后翻，铅笔字零零星星，到一多半就没了，后头干干净净，像写字的人有一天合上书走了，再没回来。

六点二十，走廊里传来钥匙响，一个保安提着手电，看见铁栅门里头站着两个人，吓得手电差点掉了。
story.en:
Shen Mang stood up. His crutch had slid under the table; he groped twice and couldn't find it. From here to the washroom meant going round two rows of shelves and a table, with everything Ma Xiaobao had tipped out lying on the floor in between.

That right foot had been sprained five days ago.

These last days he had stood on one foot in the dorm every day with his eyes shut, holding the desk, while Old Cai counted from the top bunk: three seconds, six, eleven — this morning, fifteen. Eyes shut, the brain couldn't see; all it could do was listen to the wires in the foot.

Now, eyes open or shut, it was all the same.

Holding the desk edge, he took the first step. The right foot landed and the ankle tilted outward — he felt it. The wire reported the tilt, and the leg pulled itself back and steadied. Second step. On the third his instep kicked Ma Xiaobao's thermos, which rolled away rattling. On the fourth his hand found the cold iron edge of a shelf. He edged along the shelf, one step, then another, counting in his head. From the washroom the breathing came faster and faster, like someone drowning in the dark.

Ninth step, the corner of the table. Tenth, round it. Eleventh, his hand found the washroom door handle.

He was standing steady. The right foot was on the floor, the ankle aching in waves, but it hadn't tilted, hadn't given. Those eleven steps he had not walked with his eyes — eyes were no use here, and there were no eyes watching him either; he had walked them on the wires in his foot. In the dark he grinned and shouted without a sound:

Done!

He pushed the door open. Ma Xiaobao was crammed into the space between the toilet and the wall, hugging his knees, shaking all over. Shen Mang felt his way down the wall and crouched beside him without touching him: "Xiaobao. Breathe with me. Out longer than in." He breathed in for four counts and out for six, loud enough to hear in the dark. Ma Xiaobao couldn't keep up, breaking off halfway through each exhale to gasp again; Shen Mang didn't hurry him, leading one breath at a time, like leading a child just learning to walk. Ten breaths, twenty. Thirty-odd breaths later Ma Xiaobao said hoarsely: "...My hands aren't numb. I thought I wasn't getting enough air, so I pulled harder."

"You were getting too much. Blow off all the carbon dioxide and your hands go numb," Shen Mang said. "Breathe out slower. Let it build back."

They sat like that, one inside the door and one outside, backs against the frame. Later, in the dark, Ma Xiaobao said that when he was small, playing hide-and-seek, he had climbed into a big wooden liquorice chest in his grandfather's warehouse and the lid had been latched from outside. It was New Year; the warehouse was locked, everyone had gone home; he spent the whole night inside. "Next morning my grandfather opened the chest and I smelled of liquorice from head to foot. My dad said: it's nothing."

Shen Mang thought of that page — "liquorice" — and the fingernail pressed white.

After a long time Ma Xiaobao said: "What happened today—"

"What happened today?" Shen Mang said. "Dark as this, I didn't see a thing."

In the dark, Ma Xiaobao gave a snort of a laugh, thick through the nose.

At six the lights came on. The climate unit hummed back to life. Shen Mang, slumped against the door frame, was woken by the glare and saw Ma Xiaobao asleep on the floor, one metre ninety-three curled up like a shrimp.

September's boxed set of the Yangxing Yanming Lu still lay open on the table; he had fallen asleep the afternoon before and nobody had put it away. In the margin of the page about breathing out were a few lines of pencil, small and hurried, the top one reading: "Tried it. Out longer than in; the heart did slow." Out longer than in and the heart slows — what Ahe had taught him in October, someone had tried at this very table decades ago. He took the borrowing card from the case and laid it alongside: the same hand as the water-blurred name from September. Turning on, the pencil thinned to a scatter and stopped a little past halfway; the rest was clean, as if the writer had closed the book one day and never come back.

At twenty past six keys rang in the corridor, and a security guard with a torch saw two people standing behind the iron grille and nearly dropped it.
